rewrites.summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected in its immediate neighbourhood. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; the capital Chisinau's Pride marches through the city centre under police protection, and police have deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters seeking to disrupt it.

Counterweights for a visitor: no accessible legal gender recognition exists for anyone (a medicalised process exists on paper but is reported not functional in practice); the predominant Orthodox Church and major politicians (including the capital's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements that colour the climate; and the breakaway separatist region of Transnistria, controlled by the neighbouring power Russia, has its own anti-LGBT “propaganda” law — travelers should treat that region as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented through a single contested case: a transgender man (registered female at birth in 1972, documents changed to male in 2007) served his sentence at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, where he says he was held alone in unsanitary cells — three years fully isolated from other detainees per a 2025 corroboration — including long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit, supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12 (the ward for detainees requiring protection) was refused and no special-unit option existed. He described staff humiliation (forced strip body searches, demeaning roll-call name-calling, bathroom-door intrusion) and said only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The penitentiary administration contested the account, replying that he was held alone at his own written request, that no rights were violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. For a visitor, the practical lesson is that a detained trans person in Moldova's system faced solitary-style isolation presented as protection, a refused protection-ward transfer, no special-unit option, and an administration that denies mistreatment — in a country that is otherwise the safest in its neighbourhood.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Context rather than visitor-facing mechanism: Moldova is on the EU accession path, which drives continued legal alignment. Legal flux: in 2013 an appeals court struck down a local “gay propaganda” ban as unconstitutional after church-led bans and protests against the anti-discrimination law; hate speech remains serious with no meaningful state response, and election-period political hate speech has risen, per the 2024 review. A recent travel feature portrays the country as slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity, with public Pride proceeding openly.

Custody-axis flux: the detainee said he would sue in Moldovan courts and the European Court of Human Rights, and the investigative outlet notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M — litigation and oversight-institution channels, not yet outcomes; the authorities publicly acknowledged that homophobia still persists in state institutions and announced staff training and stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment, an institutional acknowledgment with no enacted change on record.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The non-functional legal-gender-recognition process is resident-facing.

Resident data: an equality-body study found acceptance of LGBT+ people extremely low — 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues (social-distance score 5.7) — and marginalisation increased in 2022; in 2024 a trans woman was denied bank service over a document/appearance mismatch and the equality body confirmed discrimination.

The documented custody case is resident-facing: the detainee is a national held in the national penitentiary system at Soroca, and the solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, staff conduct and administration denial described in the two investigations all fall on residents in state custody — a visitor meets the practice only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The breakaway region of Transnistria is scored as part of Moldova de jure, but travelers should treat it separately: foreign-controlled, anti-LGBT “propaganda” law, no consular access. General poverty and corruption affect all travelers. No source addresses border-screening or document-practice for trans visitors, and no visitor-specific incident record exists to independently verify the assessment.

Prison axis: the placement finding rests on a single detainee's account that the prison administration disputes (it says the isolation was at his own written request and no rights were violated), so the disputed details are unadjudicated; no codified Moldovan rule on trans-prisoner housing, trans special units, or solitary/segregation placement is documented, and whether his planned court and European Court of Human Rights claims were filed is unverified in these sources.
rewrites.notes: rt004 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (ZdG 2024 and Observatorul de Nord 2025: a trans man held alone at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, no special-unit option, administration denial; 2025 corroboration of the isolation placement practice) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Luxembourg is exceptionally safe — among the strongest trans jurisdictions in its region. Legal gender recognition by self-determination has existed since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018) with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law — a visitor-specific impact is not documented.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented as comparatively protective: per the Justice Minister's 2015 parliamentary answer, prison staff place inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity so they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, trans-detainee situations are handled case by case, requests to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen form of address (a 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname); such cases are described as “exceptional”. No codified birth-sex placement rule, no trans special custody unit, and no solitary or administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners is documented, and the planned Uerschterhaff prison at Sanem was designed with multiple sections so detainees could be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, among these, sexual orientation — so a visitor who ends up in custody is met by case-by-case accommodation under an explicit official warning against stigmatising or isolating LGBT detainees, not by a fixed rule.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Legal trajectory: the self-determination regime replaced a long, costly judicial procedure — a bill was presented in May 2017 and parliament approved the simplified civil-status change in July 2018. In July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ action plan, criticised by local organisations for missing depathologisation and other elements. A 2019 report noted the law lacked LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances while the justice minister signalled evolution after a monitoring body's intervention.

Custody-axis context: the only prison-axis documentation is the 2015 parliamentary answer — placement following disclosed identity/need case by case, an explicit ministerial warning against solutions that would stigmatise or isolate LGBT detainees, and the Justice Ministry's statement that no statistics on LGBT prisoners are kept because disclosure cannot be compelled without unlawful privacy interference.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The self-determination legal-gender-recognition process (notably open to foreign nationals) is resident-facing administrative law. Civil-register amendment covers gender and first names; there is no nonbinary marker. An equality body and the national action plan serve residents' complaints and protections.

The documented custody practice is resident-facing: the 2015 ministerial statement describes how the national penitentiaries house resident inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity, its “exceptional” trans-detainee cases included — a visitor meets it only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Nothing material remains unresolved. One 2018 report of the parliamentary vote was paywalled, so the vote split could not be verified from the page; and no independent incident series is documented, so the absence of recorded anti-trans violence rests on a thin cited record.

Prison axis: the placement description is a single 2015 ministerial statement — no statute, regulation or case law on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in this record, and how the case-by-case practice operates in any given prison today is unverified; the Sanem prison's sectioned design was prospective in 2015 and its operation is unverified.
rewrites.notes: rt004 VIS: folded the verified prison-axis source (L'essentiel 2015 ministerial answer: identity/need-based case-by-case placement, surname-based address, no codified birth-sex rule, no special custody unit or solitary practice documented, Sanem sectioned design) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Honduras is dangerous for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the regional Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the region, outside the two largest countries.

The consequence axis of an arrest is one of the region's most dangerous documented elements: Honduras places transgender women in the men's prison system — birth-sex placement with no placement-by-gender-identity policy, documented in 2017 and independently confirmed in 2020. At the national penitentiary (Tamara), LGBTI prisoners were concentrated in the “La Isla” module beside the mentally-ill unit, where trans women were forced to cut their hair, barred from presenting as women, and denied conjugal visits; at Marcala, authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after the torture-prevention centre intervened was she isolated from the men and her belongings returned. Human Rights Watch states the practice “can lead to physical and sexual abuse,” and documents a Honduran judge's account of a trans woman raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards — prosecutors were informed and did not investigate (“There's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons”). A detained trans visitor therefore faces male-facility placement with documented sexual-violence risk and official inaction, matching the record's already severe street-level warning.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Regional comparison: a rights-law report groups this nation with neighbouring El Salvador among the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, and regional nations have long excluded trans women from femicide-justice frameworks — the pattern that made this case the leading one of its kind.

Justice-system context: documented impunity is driven by under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and intentional case mishandling — the enforcement backdrop for anyone assessing risk.

Custody-axis documentation trail: the placement practice is documented twice, five years apart — 2017 reporting by a trans activist drawing on the national torture-prevention centre (CPTRT), and Human Rights Watch's 2020 three-country report independently confirming that trans women are placed in men's prisons where abuse can follow; the judge-reported rape with guards' complicity and no prosecution is the enforcement context inside the system, not a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The court-ordered legal-gender-recognition reform (partially implemented) and the name-change process are resident-facing; the epidemic-level violence and mass asylum-seeking describe residents' situation.

Resident-facing documentation: trans people have faced police assault, extortion and worse for years, and politically visible trans people have faced threats and attacks, with at least one organiser seeking asylum abroad.

The custody practice is resident-facing: trans women held in the national penitentiaries' men's system — the “La Isla” concentration module at Tamara with its forced hair-cutting and dress suppression, the Marcala seizure of clothing and hair, and the judge-reported rape with guards' complicity and no investigation — all fall on residents in state custody; a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: how the documented gang and security-force violence applies to short-stay visitors in tourist contexts is not quantified in the current sources — gang violence affects everyone.
Unverified: no documented trans-visitor incidents appear in the current sources; the state-responsibility finding covers an individual case and signals institutional accountability rather than a visitor-specific enforcement pattern.
Prison axis: no Honduran statute, regulation or department policy fixing trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented — the placement practice rests on the 2017 and 2020 documentation; “La Isla” is a de facto concentration module rather than a codified special unit; and whether the documented practices persist as of the research date is unverified.
rewrites.notes: rt004 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (Corresponsales Clave 2017: men's-system placement, La Isla module, forced hair-cutting and clothing seizures, ad-hoc CPTRT protective isolation; HRW 2020: birth-sex men's-prison placement, judge-reported rape with guards' complicity and no prosecution) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
El Salvador demands real caution from trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years, among the lowest anywhere; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception (an exceptional security regime) with mass arbitrary detention (tens of thousands imprisoned, over 75,000 reported, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented and grim: since the state of exception began (March 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in the mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. The only documented custody case (2024 investigative reporting): a trans woman arrested in San Salvador in April 2022 was held at police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out with another trans woman for outdoor punishment drills (handcuffed, forced squatting in the sun), and denied her HIV clinic access; a judge freed her after about four months, finding the arrest unsupported, while the second trans woman remained imprisoned. The state-of-exception risk mechanism is therefore not hypothetical in custody: it is where the regime's arbitrary power meets identity-based mistreatment, with no special custody provision documented and release dependent on judicial review.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Regional comparison: a 2020 human-rights report groups this nation with two neighbouring nations as failing to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, driving asylum claims abroad.

Legislative and research context: 2015 legal-code reforms made bias-motivated killings punishable by long prison sentences; a 2024 longitudinal study profiles homicides against LGBTI+ people across two decades; and the first conviction came in 2020 — legal milestones that do not by themselves change the practical visitor risk.

Custody-axis context: the human-rights organisations documenting the 2022 case (Socorro Juridico Humanista, Cristosal) link the abuse to the absence of a Gender Identity Law — an explanatory framing, not a policy change — and the case's single recourse point (a judge releasing the detainee for an unsupported arrest while her co-detainee stayed imprisoned) is partial judicial pushback within an otherwise exceptional regime, not a protection a visitor can rely on.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The administrative name-change-only process and the absent legal-gender-recognition law are resident-facing; the historical life-expectancy figure and the killing case described in the summary are resident-facing too.

The documented custody case is resident-facing: the two trans women held after the April 2022 raid (one released by a judge after about four months, the other still imprisoned per the 2024 report) were residents in national custody, and the forced head-shaving, punishment drills and denied HIV clinic access fall on residents; a visitor meets the practice only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the exceptional security regime is applied to trans visitors in practice — its trans-specific application is a risk mechanism, not a documented pattern, and the regime affects all travellers.
Unverified: the sources document no trans-visitor incidents, and the historic danger figures describe residents' experience before the recent crackdown.
Prison axis: the custody documentation is a single 2024 investigation of one case — no Salvadoran statute, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) appears in this record, no special custody provision is documented for prisoners captured in the raids, and how widespread the documented mistreatment is across the mass-detention population is unverified.
rewrites.notes: rt004 VIS: folded the verified prison-axis source (GatoEncerrado 2024: raid-captured trans women held in the ordinary system with no gender-identity accommodation; forced head-shaving, outdoor punishment drills, denied HIV clinic access; judicial release of one while the other remained imprisoned) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Turkey presents real, structured danger for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become state policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 detained in Istanbul in July 2025), trans women have historically been frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration. The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (Istanbul's Beyoğlu/Tarlabaşı) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades.

The consequence axis of an arrest is severe and current: Turkey holds trans prisoners in gendered facilities by registered sex — a transgender man was held in a women's prison — and a 2024 system-level profile documents LGBTI+ prisoners facing arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation in solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, frequent transfers, and complaints that are ineffective and can lead to further violence, with no policy or staff training to address LGBTI+ needs in a system described as built on a binary, heteronormative model. The December 2025 death of a transgender prisoner in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison moved the question to formal state-level contestation: rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to “detention practices affecting transgender prisoners,” accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers describe four trans inmates sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, a delayed medical response, investigators entering only two days later and witness statements not taken, and the case was raised in parliament on 12 December 2025. For a trans visitor — already profiled and detained for identity checks — arrest means placement by registered sex in a gendered facility under practices documented as segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched housing, in a system where the most recent custody death is under contested official handling.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The October 2025 draft law is not yet enacted — its status is unresolved and under active government consideration, which colours but does not change a visitor's legal position. Turkey stands outside the Schengen border-control framework of its European neighbours, so border and transit controls follow a different regime. A foundational 2008 human-rights report documented a long history of beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people — dated context rather than current street-level risk.

Custody-axis context: the 2024 system-level documentation comes from a Prison Insider country profile on Turkey prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association (CISST) and using regional data, and the December 2025 case's procedural complaints (delayed medical response, late crime-scene entry, witness statements not taken) and the parliamentary question are the formal mechanisms through which trans-prisoner custody conditions are being contested at state level — the death's cause is unresolved and under investigation.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The Health Ministry is introducing regulations that may profile and restrict trans healthcare — a resident-facing regime; the men's-facility placement of trans women concerns resident detainees. The annual monitoring report records 313 violations in 2025 — roughly two-and-a-half times 2024 — dominated by detention (299 detention decisions), plus systematic privacy attacks; six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings with trans people the most affected, are resident discrimination data, not visitor statistics.

The documented custody practice is resident-facing: trans prisoners held by registered sex in gendered facilities (a trans man in a women's prison), the documented pattern of strip searches, solitary-style isolation, restricted healthcare, frequent transfers and ineffective complaints, and the December 2025 death of a transgender prisoner at Sincan Women's Prison all concern residents in state custody — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The October 2025 draft law is not yet passed — its enactment outcome is unresolved and under active government consideration. General terrorism and crime advisories affect all travellers to Turkey. No source in the record documents marriage or partner-travel exposure for visitors separately from the general criminalisation risk described above.

Prison axis: no Turkish statute or regulation codifying trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in this record — the registered-sex placement finding rests on the December 2025 reporting, the segregation-and-isolation practice on the 2024 Prison Insider/CISST profile, and the December 2025 death's circumstances are contested with the investigation outcome unresolved.
rewrites.notes: rt004 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (SCF 2025: transgender prisoner's death at Sincan Women's Prison, registered-sex placement in gendered facilities, contested custody conditions, rights-group and parliamentary contestation; Kaos GL/Prison Insider 2024: arbitrary strip searches, solitary-style isolation, restricted healthcare, frequent transfers, no LGBTI-specific policy or training) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.
